1163.title: The whole human condition
1163.hook: every person carries the whole form of the human condition (Essays 3.2)
1163.howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne often quote his line that each person carries the whole form of the human condition as the reason his self-portrait speaks to strangers.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the kidney stone: let the body groan, and keep the mind your own. Your line was patient with pain. A new week starts now.

Montaigne opens an essay in book three with a strange apology. Other writers, he says, try to shape a human being, to show what a person ought to be. He only describes one: himself, and not a very well made one. If he could make that man over, he says, he'd make him quite different, but it's done now. So why read page after page about one ordinary man with his faults and his kidney stone? His answer is a single sentence, and it's today's word.
screen: `OTHERS SHAPE A PERSON.` → `HE ONLY DESCRIBES ONE.` → `WHY READ ABOUT HIM?`

segments.voice: First, the passing. Montaigne says he doesn't paint being; he paints passing. Not a fixed portrait, but a man changing from day to day, even minute to minute. If he contradicts himself, it's because he's describing a moving thing honestly. Second, the sentence. Every person, he writes, carries the whole form of the human condition. Not a slice. The whole. A farmer, a king, a man with a stone in his side: each holds the full shape of being human, its fears and appetites, its kindness and its death. So a plain, private life isn't too small to study. It's a complete specimen. Third, two ways to hear it. Some readers hear humility: nothing in me is foreign to anyone else. Others hear dignity: nobody is a rough draft of a person, nobody is only a part. Montaigne seems to mean both. He studies himself not because he's special but because he isn't. Fourth, the stranger. At the pharmacy counter, the person ahead of you is easy to see as a back, a delay, a type. Montaigne's sentence won't allow it. That stranger carries the whole of it too: a childhood, a worry about money, a joke they tell well, a body that will one day stop. You don't have to know their story. Only that it's a whole one.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you saw recently and didn't know: a driver, a cashier, a person on the next bench. Hold their face a moment, then let the rest come in without inventing a story: they were a child once, they worry about someone, something makes them laugh. Let them be whole, and breathe with that.
The whole human condition. Montaigne's claim that every person, however ordinary, carries all of it. Today's word.
Your line: the whole of it. In the king, the farmer, the stranger at the counter, and in you. See you tomorrow.

1164.title: Of repentance
1164.hook: he distrusts dramatic repentance and prefers steady change (Essays 3.2)
1164.howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne's essay Of repentance often take from it a preference for slow, lasting changes in habit over dramatic resolutions that fade.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the whole human condition: every person, however ordinary, carries all of it. Your line was the whole of it.

New Year's Day. The gym is packed, the fridge is full of vegetables, and a list on the counter says this year everything changes. By February the list is under a takeout menu. Big turning points feel wonderful; they don't always last. Montaigne noticed something like this in himself, in the same essay as yesterday's sentence, the one called Of repentance. And his confession sounds odd under that title. He says he rarely repents.
screen: `THE LIST ON THE COUNTER.` → `BIG TURNING POINTS FADE.` → `HE RARELY REPENTS.`

segments.voice: First, what he means. Montaigne isn't bragging that he never does wrong; he has listed his own faults plainly elsewhere. He's talking about the regret that flares up, weeps, and changes nothing. A fault that has become a habit, he says, isn't undone by a sigh. Real regret would show in how he lives tomorrow, not in how loudly he feels it today. Second, the pattern within. A person needs a pattern inside, he says, a standard of their own to test their actions against. Not the crowd's applause, not a show of sorrow: a quiet inner measure that is there every day. Steady change starts there. Third, the regret of old age. When the appetites fade with age, he says, people sometimes call that repentance. He calls it weakness, not wisdom: the vice left, but the person didn't choose to change. He'd rather be good on purpose than good because he's tired. Fourth, a word about faith. Montaigne isn't arguing against anyone's practice of confession or turning back to God; he's describing his own temperament and what he trusts in himself. For him, change worth the name is slow, ordinary, and visible in habits: one small thing done differently, again and again, without a speech.
screen: `A HABIT ISN'T UNDONE BY A SIGH.` · `A PATTERN WITHIN.` · `WEAKNESS ISN'T WISDOM.` · `SLOW, ORDINARY, IN THE HABITS.` · then, large: `STEADY CHANGE.`

segments.voice: Think of one habit you'd like to shift, and make it small enough to do today, tomorrow and the day after: a glass of water before coffee, a kind word before a hard one, a little earlier to bed. No vow, no list on the counter. Just picture yourself doing it once, plainly.
Of repentance. Montaigne's essay that distrusts the big sigh and trusts the steady habit. Today's word.
Your line: steady change. A habit shifts by being done, not by being announced. Same time tomorrow.

1165.title: Friends, women, books
1165.hook: three kinds of company, and books the most constant (Essays 3.3)
1165.howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne's essay on three kinds of company often take it as a quiet inventory: friends, love, and books, each weighed for what it gives and what it costs.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was of repentance: Montaigne trusted the steady habit over the big sigh. Your line was steady change.

Who do you actually spend your hours with? Not who you'd list on a form: who's really there, day after day, when you look back over a week? Montaigne asks himself that in the next essay of book three. The French title calls it three kinds of commerce, meaning three kinds of dealings, three kinds of company. He names them without fuss: friends, women and books. Then he weighs each one honestly: what it gives, and what it costs.
screen: `WHO'S REALLY THERE?` → `THREE KINDS OF COMPANY.` → `WHAT EACH GIVES AND COSTS.`

segments.voice: First, friends. Montaigne prizes real friendship, where two minds talk freely and sharpen each other. But it's rare, he admits, and depends on finding the right person, and on that person staying. A gift of chance. Second, the company of women. Here he writes frankly, as a man of his time, about love and attraction between men and women. It is sweet, he says, it stirs the body and the feelings, but it is restless and can unsettle the mind. Readers today notice how his era frames it. What he's weighing is closeness that is lovely and never fully in his control. Third, books. This, he says, is the steadiest company. Books are there when he wants them and wait quietly when he doesn't; they don't sulk if he ignores them. They console him in solitude and help him pass dull hours. They live in his library in the tower, where he walks while he thinks, because his thoughts fall asleep, he says, if he makes them sit. Fourth, the catch. Even books have a fault: they exercise the mind and leave the body idle. So no single company is enough. A friend who talks back. A closeness that warms you, whatever shape it has in your life. Something steady on the shelf. Each feeds what the others can't.
screen: `FRIENDS: RARE, A GIFT OF CHANCE.` · `LOVE: SWEET, BUT RESTLESS.` · `BOOKS: THERE WHEN YOU WANT THEM.` · `EVEN BOOKS LEAVE THE BODY IDLE.` · then, large: `THREE COMPANIES.`

Your line: three companies. Friends by chance, love with its restlessness, books always on the shelf. Until tomorrow.

1166.title: Montaigne travels
1166.hook: Montaigne loved travel for the new and the different (Essays 3.9)
1166.howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne's essay Of vanity often take from it his love of unplanned travel, his curiosity about other people's customs, and his line about knowing what he flees but not what he seeks.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was friends: the first of Montaigne's three companies, rare, a gift of chance. Your line was three companies.

A traveler stands at a fork in the road. On the right, the way looks ugly, so he takes the left. That's the whole plan. No route marked, no list of sights, no deadline. If he gets somewhere he doesn't like, he leaves; if he forgot to see something, he goes back. This is Montaigne on the road, in a long, wandering essay of book three called Of vanity. The man who retreated to a tower full of books also loved to leave it.
screen: `UGLY ON THE RIGHT? GO LEFT.` → `NO PLAN, NO DEADLINE.` → `THE TOWER MAN LEAVES HOME.`

segments.voice: First, the plan that isn't one. He isn't chasing a destination, so he can't be late for it. The road itself is the point. Second, the new and the different. Travel, he says, is good exercise for the mind, kept busy noticing what it hasn't seen before. Other people's ways of eating, dressing and greeting show him the wide variety of human lives, and loosen the grip of his own habits. Third, the travelers he laughs at. He pokes fun at people who go abroad only to find their own countrymen, eat their own food and complain about everything foreign. That misses the point of going. He would rather sit at a stranger's table and eat what they eat. Fourth, the honest answer. People ask what he's looking for on these trips. He answers, more or less, that he knows well what he's fleeing, but not what he's seeking. It's a strangely freeing confession: not every journey needs a goal written down before it begins. Sometimes it's enough to need a change of air and trust the road to show you something. None of this needs a plane. A different street to the store, a neighborhood you always drive past. The mind wakes up a little when it meets something it didn't expect.
screen: `NO FIXED ROUTE.` · `EXERCISE FOR THE MIND.` · `DON'T GO ABROAD TO FIND HOME.` · `I KNOW WHAT I FLEE, NOT WHAT I SEEK.` · then, large: `A NEW ROUTE.`

segments.voice: Picture a trip you make most days, to work, the store or the mailbox, and then one small change: a different turn, a different street, a different door. Don't pick a destination, just the turn, and let your mind wander down that street, curious. If it drifts back to the usual road, take the left again.
Montaigne travels. No fixed route, a stranger's table, and a mind kept awake by the new. Today's word.
Your line: a new route. Knowing what you're leaving can be enough to set out. See you tomorrow.

1167.title: The mayor and Montaigne
1167.hook: elected mayor of Bordeaux, he says the mayor and Montaigne were always two (Essays 3.10)
1167.howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne often quote his line that the mayor and Montaigne were always two as a picture of doing a public role fully while keeping the self distinct from it.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Montaigne travels: no fixed route, a stranger's table, a mind kept awake. Your line was a new route.

The man who walked away from public life to sit in a tower with his books gets called back. The city of Bordeaux elects him mayor, and Montaigne takes the job. Then, in an essay of book three about managing your own will, he says something like a riddle: the mayor and Montaigne have always been two, clearly separated. Same body, same signature, same house. Two. What could that mean, and why would anyone want it?
screen: `BORDEAUX CALLS HIM BACK.` → `HE TAKES THE JOB.` → `THE MAYOR AND MONTAIGNE: TWO.`

segments.voice: First, the part in a play. We should play our part well, Montaigne says, but as a part, a borrowed character. The mask is real and the work is real, but the mask isn't the face. He warns against people who let the office soak into them, who become their title all the way down and carry it home to the dinner table. Second, how deep the job goes. He'll take the city's affairs into his hands, he says, but not into his lungs and liver. He'll carry the work; he won't let it eat him. That isn't laziness; it keeps him clear enough to do the work well. Third, the critics. Some said his time as mayor left little mark, that he was too easygoing. He doesn't hide it. He answers that he kept things calm, did no harm, and didn't stir up trouble just to look busy. Readers can judge whether that's enough, but he's honest about the trade he chose. Fourth, why two matters. When the role and the person are fused, every attack on the work feels like an attack on the self, and losing the job feels like losing who you are. When they're two, you can give the role your best and still go home as yourself. Manager, nurse, parent on duty, the one who always fixes things: do it fully, then take off the badge.
screen: `PLAY THE PART AS A PART.` · `IN THE HANDS, NOT THE LIVER.` · `HONEST ABOUT HIS CRITICS.` · `GIVE YOUR BEST, GO HOME AS YOU.` · then, large: `TWO, NOT ONE.`

The mayor and Montaigne. A role worn fully, and a self kept distinct underneath it. Today's word.
Your line: two, not one. The coat waits by the door, and you walk in as yourself. Rest well.

1168.title: Of cripples
1168.hook: he warns against being too sure, especially when condemning people as witches (Essays 3.11)
1168.howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne's essay Of cripples often remember it for its warning against condemning people on uncertain grounds, and for his love of softening words like perhaps and I think.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the mayor and Montaigne: a role worn fully, a self kept apart. Your line was two, not one.

Perhaps. In some sense. Some. They say. I think. Montaigne writes that he loves these little words, the ones that soften a sentence and take the swagger out of it. An odd thing to love; they don't sound brave. The essay where he says it, in book three, carries an old English title, Of cripples, taken from a passage near its end about a common saying. But much of it is about something far heavier: what happens when people are too sure, and someone else pays for it.
screen: `PERHAPS. SOME. I THINK.` → `WORDS THAT SOFTEN.` → `WHEN SURE GETS DANGEROUS.`

segments.voice: First, how stories grow. People would rather explain a strange event than check whether it happened, Montaigne notices. They skip past the facts and argue carefully about the causes. And each time a tale is passed along, it grows a little, because the teller wants to convince. Second, the witches. In his time, people accused of witchcraft were put on trial and burned. Montaigne says he was shown some accused people himself, and his judgment was gentle and blunt at once: they seemed more in need of medicine than of execution. Then the sentence this essay is remembered for, roughly: it is putting a very high price on our guesses to roast a person alive because of them. Third, the little words again. Now perhaps and I think sound different. They aren't weakness; they're a brake. He'd like the young to be taught to answer with words like: what does that mean? I don't understand it. It could be. Better to sound like a learner than certain too soon. Fourth, closer to home. Few of us will sit in judgment at a trial, but we judge all the time: a neighbor's motive, a stranger's character, a relative's choices, often from a story that grew as it passed along. His question still works. How sure am I, really? Sure enough for what it would cost them if I'm wrong?
screen: `STORIES GROW AS THEY'RE PASSED.` · `MEDICINE, NOT THE FIRE.` · `A HIGH PRICE ON OUR GUESSES.` · `HOW SURE AM I, REALLY?` · then, large: `NOT SO SURE.`

1169.title: Plague years
1169.hook: during the plague, he fled his home with his family and admired the calm of peasants facing death (Essays 3.12)
1169.howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne's essay Of physiognomy often remember his account of the plague, and his admiration for country people who met death with a calm no book had taught them.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was of cripples: Montaigne's essay against being too sure when someone else will pay. Your line was not so sure.

The plague reached the country around Montaigne's house. He writes about it in book three, in an essay called Of physiognomy. He gathered his family and left home, looking for somewhere safe. It wasn't easy: a family fleeing the plague frightened the people they hoped would take them in. Friends grew wary; hosts grew nervous at any sign of illness. The man who wrote so calmly about death in his tower now faced it on the road, with his household behind him. And what he noticed most, he says, wasn't the scholars. It was the farmers.

segments.voice: First, what he saw. The country people faced the sickness, he writes, with a plainness that stunned him. The grapes were left hanging on the vines as people readied themselves for death without drama. He tells of a man, still healthy, already digging his own grave, and of others who lay down in theirs while still alive. Grim pictures, but what struck him was the quiet in them. Second, calm without books. Montaigne had spent a long time reading philosophers on how to prepare for death. These people had read none of it, and met death more steadily than the learned. He doesn't romanticize their hardship; he's honest that their calm wasn't borrowed from a library. Third, nature as teacher. If you don't know how to die, he writes, roughly, don't worry: nature will teach you fully when the moment comes. Then a line that turns it around: we trouble our life with worry about death, and our death with worry about life. Fourth, plain and brave. The title points to faces, and he spends much of the essay on Socrates, whose face was plain, even ugly by his account, and whose courage was not. No show, no speech, just steadiness. The bravest person you know may not be the loudest. And if thoughts of death weigh on you now, you don't have to hold them alone: in the US you can call or text 988, and wherever you are, local emergency help is there.
screen: `THEY FACED IT PLAINLY.` · `CALM WITHOUT A LIBRARY.` · `NATURE WILL TEACH YOU.` · `PLAIN FACES, STEADY HEARTS.` · then, large: `THE PEASANTS' CALM.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who carried something hard without making a show of it: a grandparent, a nurse, a friend who kept going through an illness or a loss. Remember one ordinary thing they did in the middle of it, making tea, going to work, telling a joke, and let that small, steady act be your teacher for these minutes.
Plague years. Montaigne on the road, learning steadiness from people who had read none of the books he had. Today's word.
Your line: the peasants' calm. A week with Montaigne: the whole human condition, steady change, three companies, a new route, two not one, not so sure, and the peasants' calm. That's the week.
